h1: The 6 Best Zipper Pulls for Arthritis of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Zipper Pulls for Arthritis: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 6 zipper pull and button hook tools for stiff hands, scored on handle width, grip texture, hook shape and portability.
summary: The Vive Button Hook with Finger Hole is our top pick because the finger loop keeps the handle from slipping when your grip is weak. The Fanwer 2 Pack suits anyone who wants the widest, ribbed handle to fill the palm. For travel, the Buiqnpe is the small one that rides in a pocket. All six cost under $25, so the real choice is handle shape, not money.
intro: A thin plastic zipper pull looks like the obvious fix for stiff fingers, and it is the wrong one. The tool is not hard to hook onto a zipper; it is hard to hold. A slim handle forces a tight pinch, which is exactly the grip that aching joints dislike. Handle width and surface texture matter more than the hook at the business end.

We ranked six button hook and zipper pull tools on the Primea framework: handle width and texture, how the hook is shaped for zippers, the wire loop for buttons, and how well each tool travels. Every pick here is a simple hand tool under $25. They help with dressing; they do not treat any condition, and an occupational therapist can advise on bigger needs.

products.name: Vive Button Hook with Finger Hole
products.verdict: A wide cushioned handle with a finger hole. The most controlled grip in the ranking.
products.description:
Vive adds something no other tool here has: a finger hole through the handle. Slide a finger in and the tool stays attached to the hand even when grip strength fades. The handle is wide and cushioned and latex-free, the zipper hook is rounded steel and the loop is slim steel wire with a tapered tip.

That finger hole is why it beats the plain wide handles below. The Fanwer ribbed model is a similar width, but it relies on your fingers closing to hold on, while the Vive does not. It also carries a 60-day guarantee. The trade is that the zipper hook is narrow, so very small zipper tabs can be fiddly.

It is the one to buy if a plain handle slips from your grip. The caveat is that it comes singly, not in a multi-pack.
pros: Finger hole keeps tool in hand
products.idealFor: People whose hand slips on a plain handle and who want the most controlled grip.
products.skipIf: You want spares for several coats and bags.

products.name: Fanwer Button Hook with Zipper Pull, 2 Pack
products.verdict: An extra-wide ribbed handle that fills the palm. Two tools, one-handed use.
products.description:
Fanwer's two-pack has an extra-wide, ribbed handle with a non-slip massage texture and a slim steel wire loop. The listing stresses one-handed use, and you get two tools for the under $25 bucket.

It takes second because it solves the width problem without the Vive's finger loop. A wide ribbed handle spreads pressure across the palm instead of loading the fingertips, which is the point for sore joints. Against the Fanwer 3 Pack, the handle here is wider and more textured, though you lose one tool from the bundle.

A good fit for a user who wants to leave one tool at the bed and one in the coat. The caveat is that a wide handle takes more room, and it will not slide into a small pocket or purse like the Buiqnpe.
products.idealFor: People who want a wide, textured handle that fills the palm.
products.skipIf: You need a tool small enough to carry in a pocket.

products.name: Fanwer Button Hook and Zipper Pull 3 Pack
products.verdict: Three cushioned tools with a sturdy metal zipper hook. Buy for the closet, coat and suitcase.
products.description:
This Fanwer bundle includes three tools, each with a soft, textured cushioned handle, a stainless steel wire loop with a tapered tip and a sturdy metal zipper hook. All three are in the under $25 bucket.

The quantity is the argument. Leaving a tool in the bedroom, the coat closet and the travel bag means you never fetch it, and for sore hands that matters. It sits behind the 2 Pack because its handle is not described as extra-wide, so palm support is less pronounced. The sturdy metal hook is a plus where a zipper pull tab is stiff.

Choose it for a household that wants spares. The caveat is the handle: slimmer than the 2 Pack, so check it suits your grip.
cons: Three tools may be more than needed
products.idealFor: Households that want a spare tool in the closet, coat and suitcase.
products.skipIf: A slim handle is hard for your hand to hold.

products.name: Buiqnpe 2-in-1 Button Hook and Zipper Pull
products.verdict: A compact 304 stainless steel tool with an integrated hook. Rides in a pocket or purse.
products.description:
Buiqnpe sizes down. The loop is 304 stainless steel, the body is compact enough for a pocket or handbag, the handle is ergonomic and non-slip, and the zipper hook is built in. It sits in the under $25 bucket.

It ranks fourth because small is the trade. A compact handle gives your hand less to hold than the wide Fanwer or the Vive's finger hole, which defeats part of the purpose if grip strength is the main problem. Where it wins is availability: a tool that lives in your bag is used, and one in a drawer is not.

Good for travelers and for dressing away from home. The caveat is that anyone with a significant loss of grip should choose a larger handle.
cons: Small handle is harder to hold
products.idealFor: Travelers and anyone who wants a tool in a pocket or purse at all times.
products.skipIf: Weak grip means you need a wide, cushioned handle.

products.name: LYIGEOL Button Hook with Zipper Pull, 2 Pack
products.verdict: A foldable stainless head that tucks away in a bag. Two tools, one-handed use.
products.description:
LYIGEOL gives you two tools with a foldable stainless steel head and an included zipper hook, all in the under $25 bucket. Folding the head protects the hook when the tool is in a bag and keeps the sharp end from catching on fabric.

The folding hinge is a feature and a risk. It protects the hook, but a joint adds a point that can loosen over time, and it is something a hand with limited dexterity must unfold. For that reason it ranks fifth, below fixed tools whose heads never move. The listing does not describe the handle's width or texture, so palm support is less certain.

It suits travelers who want the hook covered. The caveat is a missing handle description, so check the product images.
cons: Hinge adds a point of wear
products.idealFor: Travelers who want the hook protected when the tool is in a bag.
products.skipIf: Unfolding a small hinge is itself difficult for your hands.

products.name: Plynthix 2 Pack Button Hook with Zipper Pull
products.verdict: Two tools in black and grey with a wide massage-texture handle. A low-risk starter.
products.description:
Plynthix packs two tools, one in black and one in grey, each with a wide non-slip handle in a massage texture. The loop is slender steel with a tapered tip, and the zipper hook is narrow and rounded. Cost falls in the under $25 bucket.

It ranks last because it overlaps with the Fanwer 2 Pack, which is described as extra-wide and ribbed, and it adds nothing the Vive does not do better. The two colours are a practical touch for telling tools apart in a household, but that does not change how the handle feels. The narrow zipper hook can be fiddly with small tabs.

Good for a first try with an inexpensive pair. The caveat is that it has no feature that sets it apart.
products.idealFor: First-time buyers who want two working tools without a big outlay.
products.skipIf: You want a finger loop or a very wide ribbed handle.

methodology.title: Handle width and texture
methodology.description: A wide, textured handle spreads pressure across the palm. We compared the width and surface described for each tool.

methodology.title: Grip security
methodology.description: Features that keep the tool in hand, such as a finger hole or ribbing, earned credit over plain smooth handles.

methodology.title: Zipper hook design
methodology.description: We scored hook shape and metal, since a narrow hook struggles with small tabs and a sturdy one grips stiff zippers.

methodology.title: Button loop
methodology.description: Steel loop material and tip shape decide how reliably the tool threads a button.

methodology.title: Portability and pack size
methodology.description: Pocket size, folding heads and multi-packs decide whether the tool is at hand when needed.

whatMatters.detail: A wider handle lets the whole palm take the load instead of a tight pinch between thumb and fingertips, which is the grip that sore joints dislike most. Compare the descriptions: extra-wide on the Fanwer 2 Pack, wide on the Vive, compact on the Buiqnpe. Look at the product photo beside a coin or a hand.

Something must stop the handle sliding when grip strength drops. A finger hole, as on the Vive, keeps the tool attached to the hand, while ribbing and massage textures add friction. Read the listing for these words, and avoid smooth thin plastic handles, which slip first when hands are weak, damp or cold from a winter morning outdoors.

The hook has to catch a zipper tab and pull without the tab slipping off. A rounded steel hook, as on the Vive and Plynthix, is gentle on fabric, and a sturdy metal hook such as the Fanwer 3 Pack handles stiff tabs. Check the hook is metal, and ask whether the tab on your coat is small.

The wire loop threads through the buttonhole and pulls the button back. Stainless steel resists bending and rust, and a tapered tip finds the hole more easily. The Buiqnpe names 304 stainless steel. Look for a named steel and a tip description, and note that very thick coat buttons need a sturdier loop than a thin shirt button does, so match the tool to your wardrobe.

A tool you cannot find is no help, so spares in the bedroom, coat closet and suitcase beat a single perfect tool. Packs of two or three cost little. Check the count in the title, and remember that compact tools such as the Buiqnpe suit pockets while wide ones suit a nightstand, so many households end up buying one of each.

faq.q: Do these work on all zippers?
faq.a: They work on zippers with a pull tab or hole. The Vive's rounded hook suits most coat tabs, while the Fanwer 3 Pack's sturdy metal hook is better on stiff ones. Very small tabs can be fiddly with the narrow Plynthix hook.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake?
faq.a: Choosing the smallest, lightest tool because it looks easy. A compact handle like the Buiqnpe's gives sore hands less to hold. Pick the widest handle you can store, then buy a small spare for travel.

faq.q: Is the Vive worth it over a multi-pack?
faq.a: If your grip slips, yes. The finger hole keeps the tool attached to your hand, which a cushioned handle on the Fanwer 3 Pack cannot do. If grip is fine, the multi-pack gives more tools for the same under $25.

faq.q: How do I use a button hook?
faq.a: Pass the wire loop through the buttonhole, hook the button's shank, and pull it back through. For zippers, loop the hook through the tab and pull up. The Fanwer 2 Pack is built for one-handed use, which suits most dressing.

faq.q: How do I clean and care for them?
faq.a: Wipe the handle with a damp cloth and dry the steel loop to keep it bright. Check wire loops for bends, since a bent tip will not thread. The LYIGEOL's folding hinge needs an occasional check for looseness.

faq.q: Can I use one if I have no grip at all?
faq.a: These tools assume some hand function. The Vive's finger hole helps with weak grip, but if you cannot close the hand, ask an occupational therapist about dressing aids with built-up or strapped handles, since a hand tool cannot make up for a missing grip.

finalTake: The Vive Button Hook with Finger Hole earns first place because the finger loop solves the real problem, which is keeping the tool in a weak hand. The Fanwer 2 Pack is the pick when a wide ribbed handle matters more, and the Buiqnpe covers pockets and travel. Buy a pack of spares so a tool is always within reach.
